name: Whole brain emulation
headline: Could *whole brain emulation* improve AI alignment or preserve human agency?

intro.text: Whole brain emulation would create digital minds derived from human brains. We assess the claim that those minds would improve alignment or preserve human agency. How exactly they would do that is still unresolved, and so are WBE's feasibility and its welfare implications.

basis.text: Value inheritance and human-derived oversight are argued by S16 and partly S14, but S13 judges the WBE-safety arguments flawed and S13 and S21 expect other AI first. Technical capability is shown only for 1 mm³ of cortex (S16), and value drift is raised by S16 and S21. Every pathway has a contrary or conflicting necessary link and otherwise rests on argument or assumption. Low confidence: no source tests any alignment link.

what_would_change.text: Direct evidence that a WBE-based system solves a specified alignment problem better than a non-WBE comparator.

basis.text: Three independent book-length arguments (S20, S21, S22) predict displacement of biological workers and wage pressure on emulations. None proposes a mechanism that preserves biological humans' bargaining power, and the ownership gate is not passed.

Severity follows from unbounded copy numbers and subjective speed (S22). No source estimates likelihood. Harms are hard to detect and hard to reverse once copies exist; proposed safeguards are principles only (S22).

alternatives.text: Conventional alignment research may solve the relevant problems sooner.
WBE may end up advancing AI capabilities more than safety.
Regulatory, moral and technical bottlenecks may keep it from being deployed in time. S02 points to the regulatory and moral bottlenecks explicitly.
S13 presents brain emulation as one of several underdeveloped NeuroAI pathways, and makes no case that it's an established safety solution.

intervention.text: Whole brain emulation: scanning a specific human brain at sufficient resolution and running a computational model that reproduces that person's cognition (stages S1 component simulation → S6 deployed populations). Systems that model only parts of a brain are not treated as WBE (e.g., partial emulation and digital twins, stages S1-S2).

deployment_scenario.text: WBE-O AI overseer · WBE-R alignment researcher · WBE-G general-purpose AI system · WBE-L digital labour · WBE-I institutional decision-making (provisional)

affected_groups.text: Claimed beneficiaries: humanity at large via aligned intelligence (WBE-O/R/G); owners of scans, emulations and compute (WBE-L). Bear risks: emulated persons (copying, deletion, subsistence); biological workers (displacement); scanned originals (consent); everyone (capability spillover).

time_horizon.text: Long (> 15 y). No source dates S3; S13: whole-brain simulation 'many years out'; S21: de novo AI plausibly first.

comparator.text: Alignment: conventional (non-neuro) alignment and oversight methods (S28). Intelligence Curse: labour-replacing AI without WBE.

problems_claimed.text: Alignment: value specification (WBE-G), scalable oversight (WBE-O), research acceleration (WBE-R). Intelligence Curse: claimed by no source as a benefit; displacement argued (S20-S22).

mechanism.text: Relocates the problem: value specification becomes the fidelity and stability of emulated humans; oversight becomes aligning the overseer (S13, S16, S21). Creates new agents whose alignment, welfare and governance are open (S16, S21, S22).

reason.text: Value inheritance and human-derived oversight are argued by S16 and partly S14, but S13 judges the WBE-safety arguments flawed and S13 and S21 expect other AI first. Technical capability is shown only for 1 mm³ of cortex (S16), and value drift is raised by S16 and S21. Every pathway has a contrary or conflicting necessary link and otherwise rests on argument or assumption. Low confidence: no source tests any alignment link.

decisive_question.text: Can an emulation reproduce and keep specified values or oversight judgement, and would it arrive before other advanced AI?

scenarios.gap: No entry addresses supervising a more capable system (WBE-O-L4) or compares with non-WBE oversight (WBE-O-L5).

scenarios.mechanism: Accelerated emulated researchers multiply alignment research
scenarios.gap: Only an assumed claim that depends on fidelity (S16); no comparison with AI research agents.

scenarios.mechanism: Values inherited from the original, so values need not be specified
scenarios.gap: Value inheritance argued (S16) and disputed (S13); drift raised (S16, S21); timing contrary (S13, S21).

mechanism.text: No source claims an agency-preserving mechanism. Argued effects come from digital labour; institutional use has no evidence.

answer.text: Owners of scans, emulations and compute, and asset holders if property rights hold, gain (S20). Biological workers and emulated persons lose (S20-S22).

questions.question: Who owns infrastructure, data and returns

answer.text: Not specified: scans, compute and exit unaddressed; returns go to asset holders only (S20, unverified).
Deepens replacement: emulation labour substitutes for biological labour (S20, S21); digital populations may dilute transfers and political power (S22).
Not shown; no source compares with the comparator.

reason.text: Three independent book-length arguments (S20, S21, S22) predict displacement of biological workers and wage pressure on emulations. None proposes a mechanism that preserves biological humans' bargaining power, and the ownership gate is not passed.

agency.mechanism: Emulation labour undercuts wages; humans cannot compete (S20, S21). Argued only; S20 qualifies this through asset ownership.
Selection for productive, copy-willing emulations; subsistence pay (S20, S21).
agency.ownership_questions: Can an emulation leave, refuse work or move compute provider? No.

agency.mechanism: Asset-holding humans could live on returns (S20, unverified).
agency.ownership_questions: Who owns the scans? No (S16 does not cover ownership). Who owns the emulations? Partly: emulations act as economic agents, human asset ownership assumed (S20, unverified). Can emulations own assets? No.

agency.mechanism: Transfers diluted toward digital subsistence (S22); returns to asset holders only (S20).
agency.ownership_questions: Who receives returns from emulation labour? Partly: asset holders (S20, unverified); transfers diluted (S22).

agency.mechanism: Rapidly copying digital minds could gain majority control (S22); concentration of power listed (S16). Influence through emulations is not biological-human influence.

artificial_minds_by_stage.consciousness: Agnostic. S22 assumes suitably designed digital minds could be conscious but commits to no theory; S16 notes uncertainty only during testing.
artificial_minds_by_stage.moral_status: Psychological capacities and potentials, not a single property (S22)
artificial_minds_by_stage.identity: The emulation is a distinct entity from the original person (S22)
Copies are counted individually (S22); copies made on demand and groups of copies may count as moral entities (S21); groups of copies also come up in S20 (book not yet read)
artificial_minds_by_stage.welfare: Selection for compliance, long hours, low pay; open whether lives are worth living (S21)

artificial_minds_by_stage.identity: Engineering an emulation's values is raised (S22); consent to modification not addressed (S16)
Rapid copying changes resource and voting claims (S22)
artificial_minds_by_stage.welfare: Lives below subsistence as transfers are diluted, or minds with cheap well-being (S22); subsistence wages and deletion of short-lived copies (S20, unverified)
artificial_minds_by_stage.protections: Resource bargains; avoid creating lives not worth living (S22)

exposed.text: Emulated persons; scanned originals; biological workers; everyone (capability spillover, value drift)

harms.text: Suffering across copies; copying, modification or deletion without consent; subsistence and selection; labour displacement; political dominance of digital minds; value drift; information hazards (R01-R06, R20, R21)

rationale.text: Severity follows from unbounded copy numbers and subjective speed (S22). No source estimates likelihood. Harms are hard to detect and hard to reverse once copies exist; proposed safeguards are principles only (S22).

name: Brain-computer interfaces
headline: Could *brain-computer interfaces* improve AI alignment or preserve human agency?

intro.text: Brain-computer interfaces connect the nervous system to a computer. Implanted devices already let a small number of people with paralysis move a cursor or produce text. The bigger claim is that much faster interfaces could keep people in charge of increasingly capable AI and keep their work worth paying for.

claims_to_solve.text: Alignment. One argument is that if people are tightly linked to AI systems, the systems will act as extensions of human intent and won't become separate agents with goals of their own.
The Intelligence Curse. A person working through a fast interface might do more than either a person or an AI alone, so human work would still be worth paying for as AI improves.

mechanism.text: Implanted or wearable devices record brain activity and decode it into commands, text or speech. More advanced devices also write information back by stimulating neurons.
The argument goes that with enough bandwidth, people could follow and steer an AI's reasoning as it happens and have a say in each important decision.

strongest_case.text: Of the three technologies on this site, BCIs are the most concrete. Implants already restore some movement and communication in clinical trials, so the basic technology exists and is getting better.
A person stays in the loop by design, because the system acts on someone's intentions.
Medical demand pays for progress, since restoring movement and speech is worth doing whether or not the alignment argument holds.

strongest_objections.text: Bandwidth may not be the bottleneck. The hard part of overseeing AI is understanding what it's doing, and a faster channel into a human brain doesn't obviously make that easier.
A company, a government or the AI itself could use a device that writes to the brain to monitor the person wearing it, or to manipulate or pressure them.
Access is likely to be unequal. If enhancement is expensive or risky, it could widen the gap between people who have it and people who don't, which would make the Intelligence Curse worse.

basis.text: Prerequisites are shown at laboratory scale: single-trial error signals (S26), EEG-rewarded learning on robotic tasks (S25), fNIRS classification at F1 46-67% (S27). The decisive links (information gain, resistance to gaming, transfer to frontier models) have no evidence either way, and S14 argues the oversight gain is a fixed speed-up. Neither the Moderate nor the Weak condition is met.

The only agency-strengthening evidence is therapeutic and individual, not bargaining power. The enhancement pathway has no specified mechanism, access model or ownership terms (S11, S14), while workplace and state pathways weaken agency (S19, S29).

Two independent sources (S19 peer-reviewed; S29 policy paper) identify the workplace mechanism; others are argued. Employers, states and vendors hold control; consent is judged inadequate (S29). Likelihood is not assessable from the database.

artificial_minds_questions.text: If a device writes to the brain, where does the person end and the system begin? A change in mood or a decision might be hard to attribute to either one.
Should people be able to remove an interface without losing abilities, or a sense of self, that they've come to rely on?
Who owns the data a brain produces, and the device itself, if the company that made it fails?

intervention.text: Brain-computer interfaces: devices that record (read) and/or stimulate (write) neural activity and couple it to computers or AI systems; invasive and non-invasive; stages S1 passive decoding → S4 population-scale deployment.

deployment_scenario.text: BCI-D neural data for alignment · BCI-O bandwidth for oversight · BCI-E enhancement / merger · BCI-T therapeutic · BCI-W workplace · BCI-P consumer · BCI-S state/security · BCI-X representational constraint

affected_groups.text: Claimed beneficiaries: AI developers (better feedback signals); overseers; impaired persons (BCI-T); enhanced users. Bear risks: users (manipulation, mental privacy, neuroplasticity); workers (surveillance); citizens and detainees (state monitoring); non-users (inequality).

time_horizon.text: Near for BCI-T, BCI-W, BCI-P (devices in trials or on the market: FDA IDE registrations, S16, E075; workplace EEG, S19). Medium-Long for BCI-D/O/E (only toy-task or argued evidence: S24-S27, S14). S09 claims a 5-year horizon (not accessed; tier D).

comparator.text: Alignment: RLHF / RLAIF and non-BCI oversight tooling (S28). Intelligence Curse: labour-replacing AI without BCI.

problems_claimed.text: Alignment: value specification / preference elicitation (BCI-D), oversight (BCI-O), research acceleration (BCI-E). Intelligence Curse: enhancement keeps humans relevant (BCI-E, argued); disempowerment pathways (BCI-W/S/P).

alignment_assessment.problem_addressed: Value specification; oversight; research acceleration; control

mechanism.text: Partly relocates the problem: adds a feedback channel but inherits the limits of feedback-based training (S28) and adds manipulation risk (S14). No new agents, but a new attack surface on humans (S14, S16).

reason.text: Prerequisites are shown at laboratory scale: single-trial error signals (S26), EEG-rewarded learning on robotic tasks (S25), fNIRS classification at F1 46-67% (S27). The decisive links (information gain, resistance to gaming, transfer to frontier models) have no evidence either way, and S14 argues the oversight gain is a fixed speed-up. Neither the Moderate nor the Weak condition is met.

decisive_question.text: Does neural feedback add alignment-relevant information beyond explicit feedback, and does that survive optimisation pressure?

scenarios.mechanism: Neural evaluative signals as additional training feedback
scenarios.gap: Decoding and small-task training shown; no test of information gain over explicit feedback (BCI-D-L3) or of transfer to frontier models (BCI-D-L6).
Fixed speed-up argument (S14) unanswered; security contrary (S14, S16).

scenarios.mechanism: Enhanced humans do alignment research, or 'merge' with AI

mechanism.text: Enhancement keeps humans economically relevant (argued); therapy restores agency for impaired persons. Harmful pathways: workplace, state and consumer monitoring.

answer.text: Impaired persons gain individual agency; enhanced users vs non-users unclear; employers and states gain over workers and citizens (S19, S29).

questions.question: Who owns infrastructure, data and returns

answer.text: Not specified: neural-data ownership, firmware and decoder control, and returns are unaddressed (S29 leaves data ownership open).
Mixed: complements for impaired persons; enhancement presented as delaying replacement, but S14 argues the human becomes a bottleneck; monitoring deepens dependence on employers and states.
Not shown; S14 argues enhanced humans still lose to AI-only systems.

reason.text: The only agency-strengthening evidence is therapeutic and individual, not bargaining power. The enhancement pathway has no specified mechanism, access model or ownership terms (S11, S14), while workplace and state pathways weaken agency (S19, S29).

agency.ownership_questions: Can users refuse without exclusion (work, insurance, services)? Partly: limited freedom to refuse (S19); consent alone is inadequate (S29).

agency.group: Biological humans: users vs non-users of enhancement
agency.mechanism: Enhancement could keep humans competitive (S11, assumed) but may deepen inequality (S11) and still lose to AI-only systems (S14).

agency.group: Biological humans: citizens and the state
agency.mechanism: State neural monitoring to detect dissent (S29).
Clinical BCIs restore communication and movement (S03, S16). Individual agency, not bargaining power.

agency.ownership_questions: Who owns and may use neural data? No (S29 explicitly leaves it open; legal classification unclear).
Who controls device firmware and decoders? No. Is maintenance guaranteed if a device is abandoned? No (not required). Is data portable between providers? No (not required).
Who receives returns from neural data? No.

exposed.text: Users; workers; consumers; citizens and detainees; non-users; long-term users

harms.text: Manipulation through the interface; workplace neurosurveillance; state monitoring; commercial exploitation; neural-data theft; neuroplastic change; bias; inequality (R07-R14)

rationale.text: Two independent sources (S19 peer-reviewed; S29 policy paper) identify the workplace mechanism; others are argued. Employers, states and vendors hold control; consent is judged inadequate (S29). Likelihood is not assessable from the database.

name: Neuromorphic AI
headline: Could *neuromorphic AI* improve AI alignment or preserve human agency?

intro.text: Neuromorphic, or brain-inspired, AI borrows parts of how brains work, such as spiking neurons or the circuits behind empathy, without copying any particular brain. The hope is that AI built this way would learn values closer to ours, though it might mostly just make AI more capable sooner.

claims_to_solve.text: Alignment. AI that learns the way brains do might form concepts and values closer to ours, and might be easier for people to understand and predict.

mechanism.text: Neuromorphic systems copy features of brains, such as spiking neurons, learning rules that work locally, or brain-like wiring. Some run on ordinary computers, others on chips designed to work like neurons.
One version of the safety argument goes further: work out how specific brain systems give rise to social instincts like empathy and fairness, then build those into AI on purpose.

strongest_case.text: Human brains are the only systems we know of that develop general intelligence and human values together. Understanding how they do it could be more dependable than hoping values emerge from training data.
Borrowing a few mechanisms is much easier than scanning and emulating a whole brain, so this approach could matter on a realistic timeline.
Shared structure could make AI easier to inspect, since neuroscience already has decades of tools and theories for studying brain-like systems.

strongest_objections.text: A system with brain-like parts could still end up with values very different from ours if its training, body and incentives differ, and it might look more trustworthy than it is.
The insights that make AI more brain-like could also make it more capable and efficient before anyone knows how to align it, so this work may speed up capabilities more than safety.
Neuroscience doesn't yet know how brains produce values. The circuits the safety case depends on are less well understood than, say, vision or movement.

basis.text: S30 (peer-reviewed, affiliated authors) argues brain-like motivational systems make human-style safety reasoning appropriate, but also lists instability risks and notes the theories are underdetermined. The only empirical result (S13) is a small-benchmark gain, smaller than that of a non-neural method. Hardware sources concern governance, not alignment benefit (S05-S07).
No source in the database claims an Intelligence Curse benefit. 'Not claimed' is distinct from Weak or Unclear.

Governance risks are argued by preprints (S05-S07) and one peer-reviewed argument (S30). On-chip learning defeats weight inspection and countermeasures are immature. Only one risk has a likelihood judgement (S06: low for current devices).

artificial_minds_questions.text: Could a brain-like AI be conscious or able to suffer, and would brain-like hardware make that more likely than brain-like software?
If we deliberately build in social emotions like empathy, do we also build in the capacity to be hurt?
How could anyone tell from the outside whether such a system has welfare that matters, given that it might report feelings whether or not it has them?

intervention.text: Brain-inspired computing: neuromorphic hardware (spiking, in-memory, self-assembled substrates), brain-inspired AGI architectures with human-like motivational systems, and models constrained by neural data. Family boundary still open.

deployment_scenario.text: NM-H hardware / efficient compute · NM-A brain-inspired AGI architecture · NM-N neural-data-constrained models · NM-E edge / decentralised deployment

affected_groups.text: Claimed beneficiaries: AI developers (efficiency, robustness); users of edge AI. Bear risks: users and data subjects (attack surfaces); everyone (unauditable learning, escape from compute-threshold regulation, AGI value instability); brain-inspired agents if moral patients.

time_horizon.text: Near for NM-H (chips exist: S05, S07). Long for NM-A (S30 argued only). NM-N: projected compute far beyond GPT-4 for human-level robustness (S13).

comparator.text: Alignment: non-neuromorphic AI and standard robustness / interpretability methods (adversarial training: S13). Intelligence Curse: concentrated cloud AI.

problems_claimed.text: Alignment: interpretability/robustness (NM-N), value specification via motivational architecture (NM-A), verification (NM-H). Intelligence Curse: no source claims a benefit (NM-E decentralisation unclaimed).

mechanism.text: Relocates the problem: replaces objective specification with design of a motivational architecture (S30). May create new agents if brain-inspired agents have moral status; no source addresses it.

reason.text: S30 (peer-reviewed, affiliated authors) argues brain-like motivational systems make human-style safety reasoning appropriate, but also lists instability risks and notes the theories are underdetermined. The only empirical result (S13) is a small-benchmark gain, smaller than that of a non-neural method. Hardware sources concern governance, not alignment benefit (S05-S07).

decisive_question.text: Can specified motivational mechanisms be built and shown to stay stable under learning?

scenarios.mechanism: Human-like motivational architecture yields friendly behaviour
scenarios.gap: All support argued by affiliated authors (S30); stability contrary (S30).

scenarios.mechanism: Human-style reasoning predicts the system's behaviour
scenarios.gap: S30 argues verification of any AGI is intractable, which moves the problem rather than showing an advantage.

scenarios.mechanism: Neural-data constraints confer robustness or interpretability
scenarios.gap: Own experiments: adversarial training stronger; gain vanished with noise (S13).

scenarios.mechanism: No benefit claimed; the entries record verification and interpretability conditions

mechanism.text: No source claims a mechanism. Edge deployment spreading power is a hypothesis no source makes.

questions.question: Who owns infrastructure, data and returns

answer.text: Not specified: fabrication, models, deployment control and efficiency gains unaddressed (S05 notes small fabrication runs only).

reason.text: No source in the database claims an Intelligence Curse benefit. 'Not claimed' is distinct from Weak or Unclear.

agency.mechanism: No source claims an effect; S05 does not analyse power.

agency.ownership_questions: Who owns fabrication capacity? No (S05 notes small fabrication runs only). Who owns the models? No.

agency.mechanism: Edge efficiency shown (S05), but its effect on control is not analysed; efficiency is a prerequisite, not evidence about control.
agency.ownership_questions: Who controls deployment? No. Does edge deployment reduce or move dependence on concentrated providers? No (not analysed).

artificial_minds_by_stage.identity: Self-modification discussed as a safety risk, not a welfare issue (S30)

exposed.text: Users and data subjects; third parties; everyone (regulatory escape, unstable AGI values); brain-inspired agents if they have moral status

harms.text: Hardware attacks; unauditable on-device learning; escape from compute-threshold rules and export controls; opaque self-assembled hardware; unstable AGI values; unrecognised moral status (R15-R19, R22)

rationale.text: Governance risks are argued by preprints (S05-S07) and one peer-reviewed argument (S30). On-chip learning defeats weight inspection and countermeasures are immature. Only one risk has a likelihood judgement (S06: low for current devices).
